Is this argument correct? How can we be sure? In natural language we can construct reasons why this argument must be correct, although it is easy for these reasons to be restatements of the argument. In formal logic, we have mathematical tools to help us. There are several ways in which we can prove that this argument is correct, or more specifically that it is valid as we have no way to verify the truth or otherwise of the premises of the argument.We will first consider how to use truth tables to prove the correctness of an argument. Then, we will introduce a technique called
that more closely resembles mathematics to help us.

children.value: We need to ask two questions to prove that the argument is valid:
In which row of this table are all of the premises True?
Is the conclusion also True on that row?
If the Conclusion is True when all of the premises are True, then the argument is Valid.

Looking at the table, we see that in the fourth row of the table, both of the premises and the conclusion are True and therefore the argument is valid. It iw worth reminding ourselves that if the premises are also True, then the argument would be sound as well.

Natural deduction involves application of so-called

to the premises of an argument. The rules manipulate the premises in ways that are provably correct to create new statements. If the premises are True, and the rules have been applied correctly, then the consequents must also be True. We use the inference rules to perform substitions into the premises until we have arrived at the conclusion (or contradicted it), just as we do when constructing a mathematical proof. children.value: Let us explain some features of the proof
Each line of the proof consists of a single proposition.
A proposition is either a premise or results from an application of exactly one rule of inference to one or more other propositions.

When a rule of inference is applied, the propositions to which it has been applied should be stated as a subscript. For example, the application of Modus Tollens in line 4 uses propositions 1 and 2, whilst the double negation in line 5 uses proposition 4.

on which a proposition depends should be listed in the final column, regardless of whether they have been used directly in the application of a rule. For examples, line 5 does not use premises 1 and 2 directly, but they were used to derive premise 4, which does use them directly.
In sequent form, we write this as
